items.hint1: This is about Nigeria's Land Use Act of 1978 and the right it gives a person who holds a certificate of occupancy.
items.hint2: The term is a long lease, meant to cover about a person's whole working life and beyond, so the shortest figure is far too short.
items.hint3: The two long figures differ by just one year. Which exact figure does the Act set for a certificate of occupancy?
items.solution:
Answer: C. 99 years

The Land Use Act of 1978 placed land in each state under the Governor, who grants people a right to use it. The certificate of occupancy is the document for that right, and the syllabus teaches that it is granted for a term of up to 99 years.

How to tell: remember the Act's figure as a 99-year lease. It is long enough to cover a lifetime of farming or building, but it is a lease, not ownership forever.

Why not the others:
A. 20 years: far too short, and not the term set for a certificate of occupancy.
B. 59 years: not a term used under the Act.
D. 100 years: close, but the term taught is 99 years, not a full century.

Exam tip: for land law questions, link each law to its key fact: Land Use Act, 1978, land vested in the Governor, certificate of occupancy up to 99 years.

items.hint1: Ask why farm produce is plentiful at one time of year and scarce at another. What natural factor controls when most crops are grown?
items.hint2: Most crops in West Africa are grown only when the rains come. A method that removes seasonality must let farmers produce outside the rainy season.
items.hint3: Advice and good field practices raise yield, but the crop is still grown in the same season. Which option actually supplies what the dry season lacks?
items.solution:
Answer: A. practicing irrigation

Produce is seasonal because most farming depends on rainfall, so crops are grown and harvested at the same time each year. Irrigation supplies water in the dry season, so crops can be grown and harvested all year round.

How to tell: find the option that breaks the link between farming and the rainy season. Only a steady water supply does that. (Storage and processing also help even out supply, but they are not offered here.)

Why not the others:
B. better extension services: they teach farmers better methods, but production still follows the rains.
C. employing cultural cultivation practices: these improve yield within the season, not outside it.
D. exportation during scare periods: sending produce away when it is scarce would make local scarcity worse, not remove it.

Exam tip: when a question asks how to overcome seasonality, look for a way to produce out of season (irrigation) or to keep produce longer (storage, processing, preservation).

items.hint1: Think about what crop improvement tries to achieve for a farmer: better yield, better quality and fewer losses.
items.hint2: Research aims to give farmers crops with useful traits. Any option describing a weakness, such as being easily attacked, cannot be a benefit.
items.hint3: Once the harmful traits are set aside, compare the rest: is research mainly about keeping old local types, or about producing new improved ones?
items.solution:
Answer: B. develops crops that short maturity period

Agricultural research breeds improved crop varieties. Its aims include higher yield, better quality, resistance to pests and diseases, and early maturity, so farmers can harvest sooner and sometimes grow more than one crop a year.

How to tell: a short maturity period is a desirable trait, so it is a reason research is important.

Why not the others:
A. promotes the use of local varieties of crops: research mainly develops improved varieties to replace low-yielding local ones.
C. develops crops that are susceptible to local diseases: being easily infected is a weakness research tries to remove.
D. produces crops with reduced resistance to pests: research aims to increase resistance, not reduce it.

Exam tip: for any question on the aims of crop improvement or research, pick the option that is a benefit to the farmer, such as higher yield, early maturity or resistance. Options that sound harmful are distractors.

items.hint1: Each weather factor has its own measuring instrument, and the first part of an instrument's name often tells you what it measures.
items.hint2: Wind speed is measured with an anemometer and atmospheric pressure with a barometer.
items.hint3: Two options are left. One is about how long the sun shines, the other is about water vapour in the air. Think of another word that starts with 'hygro', such as hygroscopic water in soil. Which fits?
items.solution:
Answer: D. relative humility

A hygrometer measures relative humidity, which is how much water vapour is in the air compared with the most it could hold at that temperature. The option is misspelt, but humidity is what it means.

How to tell: 'hygro' means moisture, and '-meter' means a measuring instrument, so a hygrometer measures moisture in the air.

Why not the others:
A. wind speed: measured with an anemometer.
B. daylength: the hours of sunshine are recorded with a sunshine recorder.
C. atmospheric pressure: measured with a barometer.

Exam tip: learn the weather instruments as pairs: rain gauge for rainfall, thermometer for temperature, hygrometer for humidity, anemometer for wind speed, wind vane for wind direction, barometer for pressure.

items.hint1: Picture a hand fork: a short handle with several thin, pointed parts sticking out like fingers.
items.hint2: Gangs are sets of discs or tines on tractor implements, not parts of a small hand tool.
items.hint3: Of the remaining words, which one is the usual name for the pointed teeth of a fork, like those on a table fork?
items.solution:
Answer: D. prongs

The hand fork is a small garden tool used to loosen soil, break clods and remove weeds around plants. Its finger-like pointed parts are called prongs (also called tines), and they dig into and break up the soil.

How to tell: the pointed teeth of any fork, from a table fork to a garden fork, are its prongs.

Why not the others:
A. gangs: this word describes groups of discs or tines on tractor-drawn implements.
B. rings: a hand fork has no parts called rings.
C. rods: the prongs are not called rods, and the word is not used for hand fork parts.

Exam tip: for tool questions, learn each tool's main parts and what they do: a hand fork has a handle and prongs, a hoe has a blade and handle, a rake has teeth on a head.

items.hint1: This is a 'not' question. Three options are true reasons for looking after farm machines. Find the odd one out.
items.hint2: Salvage value is the money a machine is still worth when it is sold off at the end of its use. A well-kept machine is worth more.
items.hint3: Ask of each option: would a farmer want this result? The one that describes a loss to the farmer is the answer.
items.solution:
Answer: A. reduce the salvage value

Machines are maintained so that they work well, last longer and are safe to use. A machine in good condition also sells for more at the end of its life, so maintenance raises its salvage value (the value left when it is sold off).

How to tell: every true reason is a benefit. Reducing salvage value is a loss, so it cannot be a reason for maintenance.

Why not the others:
B. prolong the useful life: this is a true reason, since care stops parts wearing out early.
C. prevent avoidable accidents: a true reason, since faulty machines can injure the operator.
D. keep in good working condition: a true reason, and the main purpose of routine servicing.

Exam tip: in 'which is not a reason' questions, look for the option that describes a harmful result. Reasons for good practice are always things the farmer wants.

items.hint1: Strata are layers. Think about which of the three rock groups forms by material settling layer upon layer.
items.hint2: Igneous rocks form from cooled molten rock, not from material settling layer upon layer.
items.hint3: Three of the options are igneous rocks. The one that is sedimentary forms from shells and calcium carbonate settling in water.
items.solution:
Answer: B. limestone

Sedimentary rocks form when particles such as sand, mud or shells settle, usually in water, and are pressed together over a long time. Because the material builds up one layer on another, these rocks show strata, which means layers.

How to tell: limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from shells and calcium carbonate, so it has strata.

Why not the others:
A. gabbro: an igneous rock formed from cooled molten rock, not built up from settled layers.
C. granite: an igneous rock with crystals, not layers.
D. basalt: an igneous rock formed from lava, not built up in layers.

Exam tip: link each rock group to its feature: strata and fossils point to sedimentary rock (limestone, sandstone, shale), crystals from cooling point to igneous rock (granite, basalt, gabbro).

items.hint1: Soil water is grouped by how tightly the soil holds it. Think about which kind a root can pull out easily.
items.hint2: Water that drains quickly downwards is lost before roots can use much of it, and water stuck as a thin film on soil particles is held too tightly for roots.
items.hint3: You are left with rainwater that has not yet entered the soil and water held in the tiny spaces between particles. Which is actually stored in the soil for roots?
items.solution:
Answer: C. capillary water

Capillary water is held in the tiny pores between soil particles, against the pull of gravity. It is held loosely enough for roots to absorb, so it is the water plants mainly use.

How to tell: sort soil water by how tightly it is held. Gravitational water is held too loosely and drains away. Hygroscopic water is held too tightly. Capillary water is in between, so roots can take it up.

Why not the others:
A. precipitation water: this is rain as it falls. It only becomes soil water after it enters the soil.
B. gravitational water: it drains down through large pores soon after rain, so little is available to roots.
D. hygroscopic: this water forms a thin film stuck tightly to soil particles, and roots cannot remove it.

Exam tip: remember the three soil waters in order of how tightly they are held: gravitational (drains away), capillary (available to plants), hygroscopic (unavailable).

items.hint1: Granular structure means small, rounded crumbs of soil. Think about what binds soil into crumbs.
items.hint2: Crumbs form where there is plenty of humus, roots and soil organisms. The deep layers of weathered rock have almost none of these.
items.hint3: Compare the top layer, rich in organic matter, with the layer just below it, where clay collects in blocks. Which one has the crumbs?
items.solution:
Answer: A. horizon A

Horizon A is the topsoil. It has the most humus, roots and soil organisms, and these bind mineral particles into small rounded crumbs, which is granular structure.

How to tell: granular structure goes with organic matter and living things, and these are found mainly in the topsoil.

Why not the others:
B. horizon B: the subsoil, where clay washed down from above collects, usually giving a blocky or column-like structure.
C. horizon C: weathered parent rock with little organic matter and little developed structure.
D. horizon D: some textbooks use this for the bedrock, which is solid rock with no soil structure at all.

Exam tip: for soil profile questions, remember that the topsoil (horizon A) is the layer with the most humus, living things, crumb structure and dark colour. Features of weathered rock belong lower down.

items.hint1: Two steps: first link the symptom to the nutrient that is missing, then find the fertilizer that supplies that nutrient.
items.hint2: Purple colouring of leaves is the typical sign of a shortage of phosphorus. Yellowing points to nitrogen instead.
items.hint3: Look at the fertilizer names for a clue to the nutrient each one supplies. Only one name points to phosphate.
items.solution:
Answer: C. single superphosphate

Purple or reddish colouring of leaves is the classic sign of phosphorus deficiency. It is corrected by adding a phosphate fertilizer, and single superphosphate is a common one.

How to tell:
Step 1: purple leaves point to phosphorus (P) deficiency.
Step 2: the fertilizer that supplies phosphorus is a superphosphate.

Why not the others:
A. calcium carbonate: this is lime, used to reduce soil acidity and supply calcium, not phosphorus.
B. ammonium sulphate: supplies nitrogen and sulphur. Nitrogen shortage shows as yellow leaves, not purple.
D. muriate of potash: supplies potassium, whose shortage shows as scorched leaf edges.

Exam tip: learn the common deficiency pairs: yellowing of older leaves, nitrogen; purpling, phosphorus; scorched leaf margins, potassium. Then match the nutrient to the fertilizer name: ammonium or urea for N, phosphate for P, potash for K.

items.hint1: The name tells you where the water comes from. Think about the direction the water travels to reach the crop.
items.hint2: Water sent through buried pipes is underground irrigation, and water dripped slowly right at the root zone is drip irrigation.
items.hint3: Two options remain. Ask whether each one tells you how the water reaches the crop, or only describes something that could be true of other methods too. Which one defines water sprayed from above?
items.solution:
Answer: B. supplies water to crops on the surface of farmland

Overhead irrigation, such as a sprinkler, sprays water into the air above the crop so that it falls on the plants and the soil surface like rain. Here 'surface' only means the water lands on top of the farmland. It is not the same as what the syllabus calls surface irrigation, where water flows along the ground in furrows or basins.

How to tell: overhead means from above, so the water lands on top of the crop and the land surface, not below ground or at the roots only.

Why not the others:
A. involves the use of little volume of water: using very little water is the main feature of drip irrigation, not the definition of overhead irrigation.
C. delivers water to crops through underground pipes: this is underground (sub-surface) irrigation.
D. delivers water directly to the roots of crops: this is drip or trickle irrigation.

Exam tip: match each irrigation type to where the water goes: overhead or sprinkler, from above like rain; surface, flowing over the land in furrows or basins; underground, through buried pipes; drip, slowly at the roots.

items.hint1: First recall the main causes of agricultural pollution: chemicals and animal waste getting into soil, water and air.
items.hint2: Any option that adds farm chemicals to the land is a source of pollution, not a way to prevent it.
items.hint3: Two options are left. For each one, ask whether it keeps chemicals and animal waste away from soil and water, or brings them closer.
items.solution:
Answer: D. practicing organic farming

Much agricultural pollution comes from synthetic fertilizers and pesticides washing into rivers and soil. Organic farming uses manure, compost and natural pest control instead, so it greatly reduces this pollution.

How to tell: a preventive measure must remove a cause of pollution. Organic farming removes the use of synthetic chemicals.

Why not the others:
A. applying inorganic fertilizers to soils: excess fertilizer runs off into water and is a source of pollution.
B. spraying herbicides to control weeds: herbicides leave chemical residues in soil and water.
C. siting poultry farms near rivers: droppings and waste wash into the river and pollute it.

Exam tip: for pollution questions, sort options into causes and cures. Anything that adds chemicals or waste near water is a cause, so the answer is the option that reduces them.

items.hint1: Not every underground food store is a root. Ask what kind of organ the edible yam tuber really is.
items.hint2: A sett is a cut piece of the tuber used for planting, so it is not the name of the organ itself. Leaves make food rather than store it in yam.
items.hint3: You are left with root and stem. Think about which of these two organs normally carries buds that grow into new shoots, and where a yam's new shoots come from.
items.solution:
Answer: B. stem

In the syllabus, the yam tuber is classed as a stem tuber: a swollen underground stem that stores starch. New shoots grow from it, which is a stem feature.

How to tell: sort storage organs by crop. Cassava and sweet potato store food in root tubers. Yam and Irish potato store food in stem tubers.

Why not the others:
A. root: cassava and sweet potato are root tubers, but yam is taught as a stem tuber.
C. sett: a sett is a piece of the tuber cut for planting, not the organ where food is stored.
D. leaf: yam leaves make food by photosynthesis, but the food is stored in the tuber.

Exam tip: learn the storage organ with the crop: root tuber (cassava, sweet potato), stem tuber (yam, Irish potato), corm (cocoyam), bulb (onion), rhizome (ginger).

items.hint1: Think about what grows on harvested produce that is still damp, the kind of growth you see on bread that has been left damp.
items.hint2: Moisture control is a storage measure. Tiny worms in the soil and disease agents carried by insects inside living plants are not what drying guards against.
items.hint3: Two groups of microbes remain. Which one produces moulds and harmful toxins on damp stored produce?
items.solution:
Answer: C. fungi

Damp produce allows moulds, which are fungi, to grow on it. Some moulds, such as Aspergillus, produce aflatoxin, a poison that makes the produce unsafe to eat. Drying the crop to a low moisture content stops them growing.

How to tell: reducing moisture before harvest and storage is taught for field crops as a way to prevent mould growth and fungal toxins.

Why not the others:
A. nematodes: tiny worms that attack roots in the soil, not a contamination of dried produce.
B. viruses: they attack living plants and are spread by insects, not controlled by drying.
D. bacteria: they can cause rots, but the main contamination that drying is taught to prevent is mould.

Exam tip: when a storage question mentions moisture, damp or drying, think of moulds (fungi) and aflatoxin.

items.hint1: Blackarm is one of the bacterial diseases in the syllabus. Recall which crop each bacterial disease is linked with.
items.hint2: Blackarm causes dark lesions on the stems (the 'arms') and on the fruit of a fibre crop.
items.hint3: Which of these crops is grown for fibre from its bolls?
items.solution:
Answer: A. cotton

Blackarm, also called bacterial blight, is a disease of cotton caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas. It makes angular spots on leaves, black lesions on the stems and branches, and rots the bolls.

How to tell: blackarm is named for the black lesions on the stem and branches of the cotton plant.

Why not the others:
B. citrus: its bacterial disease in the syllabus is citrus canker.
C. yam: yam is known for yam mosaic and tuber rots, not blackarm.
D. plantain: its well-known leaf disease is sigatoka, caused by a fungus.

Exam tip: learn each named crop disease with its crop and cause: blackarm, cotton, bacterium; black pod, cocoa, fungus; swollen shoot, cocoa, virus; sigatoka, banana or plantain, fungus.

items.hint1: Think about which parts of the rice grain are removed when it is polished to make it white and shiny.
items.hint2: Polishing takes off the outer brown bran layers of the grain. Ask what those layers contain.
items.hint3: Polishing is not done to soften grains, and it cannot add grain. Of the two options left, which one follows from losing the outer layers and the germ?
items.solution:
Answer: C. reduces the nutritive value of grains

Polishing removes the bran, the thin brown outer layers of the rice grain. These layers carry much of the grain's vitamin B1, minerals and protein, so polished rice is less nutritious than brown rice.

How to tell: anything removed from the grain is lost from the diet. Removing the nutrient-rich bran lowers food value.

Why not the others:
A. reduces the hardness of grains: polishing only removes outer layers, and it is not done to soften the grain.
B. increases the quantity of grain: removing layers makes the grain lighter, so the quantity cannot increase.
D. increases the germination rate of grains: polishing removes the germ (embryo), so polished grain does not germinate well.

Exam tip: for processing questions, ask what the process removes or adds. Polishing, milling and over-refining remove outer layers and lower nutritive value, while parboiling helps keep nutrients.

items.hint1: In budding, the stock provides the roots and the lower stem. Think about which diseases attack that part of a citrus tree.
items.hint2: A rootstock can only protect the tree against a disease that attacks the part the stock supplies. Diseases of leaves, twigs and fruit attack the scion, so the stock cannot stop them.
items.hint3: Of the diseases left, which one attacks the collar and roots at the base of the tree, rather than the leaves, twigs or fruit?
items.solution:
Answer: A. gummosis

Gummosis, or foot rot, is caused by the soil-borne organism Phytophthora, which the syllabus treats as a fungus. It attacks the base of the trunk and the roots, making the bark crack and ooze gum. Sour orange resists it, so sweet orange is budded onto a sour orange stock to give the tree resistant roots and base.

How to tell: the stock is the part in the soil, so its resistance protects against a soil-borne disease of the collar and roots.

Why not the others:
B. canker: attacks leaves, twigs and fruit of the scion, so the stock cannot protect against it.
C. citrus scab: also attacks leaves and fruit, above the stock.
D. powdery mildew: not a citrus disease taught at this level, and it attacks leaves, not roots.

Exam tip: in budding or grafting questions, the stock gives the roots, so resistance from the stock is to soil and root problems, while the scion gives the fruit quality.

items.hint1: Plantation agriculture means large estates of one crop that stays on the land for many years. Think about which kinds of crops last that long.
items.hint2: Plantation crops are perennials, such as tree crops. Short-season crops harvested in a few weeks or months do not fit the plantation model.
items.hint3: For each of the three, fruits, vegetables and beverages, decide whether it is a perennial crop grown on a large permanent estate or a short-season crop grown in smaller plots, then pick the option that fits all three.
items.solution:
Answer: B. I and III

Plantation agriculture is the growing of one perennial crop, usually a tree crop, on a large estate for many years. Fruit crops such as citrus and banana, and beverage crops such as cocoa, coffee and tea, are grown this way.

How to tell:
I. fruits: perennial tree crops such as citrus are grown on plantations, so this is included.
II. vegetables: short-season crops, usually grown in market gardens, so this is left out.
III. beverages: cocoa, coffee and tea are classic plantation crops, so this is included.

Why not the others:
A. I and II: includes vegetables, which in the syllabus are market garden crops, not plantation crops.
C. II and III: includes vegetables and leaves out fruits.
D. I, II and III: includes vegetables, which do not fit the plantation system.

Exam tip: link plantation agriculture with large estates of perennial tree crops such as cocoa, oil palm, rubber and citrus. Short-season crops such as vegetables belong to market gardening.

items.hint1: Many dormant seeds have a hard coat that keeps water out. Think about how a farmer can soften or crack that coat.
items.hint2: Sterilization kills organisms, and soil treatment prepares the soil; neither acts on the seed coat to end dormancy.
items.hint3: Two options involve temperature. In the syllabus, one is used to keep stored seeds dormant and the other is used to soften hard seed coats. Which one breaks dormancy?
items.solution:
Answer: C. heat treatment

Many seeds stay dormant because a hard seed coat stops water and air getting in. Heat treatment, such as soaking in hot water, softens or cracks the coat so the seed can take in water and germinate. The syllabus lists it with scarification (scratching the coat) and acid treatment as ways of breaking dormancy.

How to tell: choose the treatment that acts on the seed coat to let water in.

Why not the others:
A. soil treatment: this prepares or disinfects the soil, not the seed coat.
B. refrigeration: some seeds from cold countries do need chilling, but in the syllabus cold storage is taught as a way to keep seeds dormant and viable, not to break dormancy.
D. sterilization: this kills germs, and harsh sterilizing can kill the embryo too.

Exam tip: for dormancy questions, look for methods that damage or soften the seed coat: scarification, soaking in hot or ordinary water, heat treatment and acid treatment.

items.hint1: Trees that fix nitrogen are usually legumes, with nodules on their roots. Look for the legume among the names.
items.hint2: Teak (Tectona grandis) and afara (Terminalia superba) are timber trees, not nitrogen-fixing legumes.
items.hint3: Of the two names left, which is the fast-growing legume that farmers cut back as hedgerows between crop rows?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Leucaena leucocephala

In alley cropping, food crops are grown in the spaces (alleys) between rows of trees that are pruned regularly. The prunings are added to the soil as mulch and green manure. Leucaena is a legume, so bacteria in its root nodules fix nitrogen, which enriches the soil for the crops.

How to tell: find the leguminous tree. Leucaena, Gliricidia and Cassia are the standard alley cropping trees in the syllabus.

Why not the others:
A. Tectona grandis: teak, a timber tree that does not fix nitrogen.
C. Terminalia superba: afara, a timber tree that does not fix nitrogen.
D. Tertulia Africana: not one of the nitrogen-fixing hedgerow trees taught for alley cropping.

Exam tip: for alley cropping or agroforestry questions, look for a leguminous tree such as Leucaena, Gliricidia or Cassia. Timber trees like teak, afara and gmelina are the distractors.

items.hint1: Ornamental plants are grouped by form: trees, shrubs, flowers and lawn grasses. Picture how Allamanda grows in a school compound.
items.hint2: A seed is a part of a plant, not a type of ornamental plant, and Allamanda is not a lawn grass.
items.hint3: Allamanda has bright yellow trumpet-shaped flowers and woody stems, and is often trained as a hedge. Does it grow from one tall main trunk, or from several stems close to the ground?
items.solution:
Answer: C. shrub

A shrub is a woody plant that is shorter than a tree and has several stems from near the ground instead of one trunk. Allamanda is a bushy ornamental with bright yellow trumpet-shaped flowers, sometimes trained to climb, and it is grown as a shrub or hedge.

How to tell: Allamanda is low, bushy and woody with many stems, which is the shrub form.

Why not the others:
A. tree: a tree has one tall main trunk, and Allamanda does not.
B. grass: ornamental grasses are for lawns, such as Cynodon, while Allamanda is a flowering woody plant.
D. seed: a seed is a plant part, not a type of ornamental plant.

Exam tip: learn ornamental examples by form: shrubs (Allamanda, Hibiscus, Ixora, Croton), climbers (Bougainvillea), shade trees (Delonix, flamboyant), lawn grasses (Cynodon, Bahama grass).

items.hint1: Fungicides kill fungi only. First recall what causes each of these diseases.
items.hint2: Cassava mosaic and cotton leaf curl are caused by viruses, which fungicides cannot kill.
items.hint3: Between swollen shoot of cocoa and sigatoka of banana, one is caused by a virus and one by a fungus. Which of the two is the fungal one?
items.solution:
Answer: D. sigatoka diseases of banana

A fungicide can only control a disease caused by a fungus. Sigatoka is a leaf spot disease of banana and plantain caused by the fungus Mycosphaerella, so it can be controlled by spraying fungicides.

How to tell: identify the cause of each disease. Only sigatoka is fungal. The other three are viral.

Why not the others:
A. cassava mosaic: a viral disease spread by whiteflies, controlled with resistant varieties and clean cuttings.
B. swollen shoot of cocoa: a viral disease spread by mealybugs, controlled by cutting out infected trees.
C. cotton leaf curl: a viral disease spread by whiteflies.

Exam tip: match the control to the cause: fungicides for fungal diseases, and for viral diseases use resistant varieties, clean planting material and control of the insect vector. Words like mosaic, swollen shoot and leaf curl usually point to a virus.

items.hint1: Dual-purpose cattle are kept for two products. Think of the two main products we get from cattle.
items.hint2: Dual-purpose here means kept for both milk and beef. Breeds kept mainly for beef or for work do not fit.
items.hint3: Which of these Nigerian breeds, kept by Fulani herders, is well known for giving milk as well as meat?
items.solution:
Answer: C. white Fulani

Dual-purpose cattle are kept for two main products, milk and beef. The White Fulani (Bunaji) is the breed Nigerian texts cite as dual-purpose, because it gives a fair amount of milk and also good beef.

How to tell: find the breed known for both milk and meat. The White Fulani is the standard example.

Why not the others:
A. muturu: a small, trypanosome-tolerant local breed kept mainly for beef.
B. keteku: a cross between Muturu and zebu cattle, classed mainly as a beef and trypanosome-tolerant breed.
D. red Bororo: kept mainly for beef and draught, with little milk.

Exam tip: learn each cattle breed with its main use: White Fulani, dual-purpose; Muturu and N'dama, beef and trypanosome-tolerant; Friesian and Jersey, dairy.

items.hint1: Sort the products by whether the animal has to be killed to get them.
items.hint2: Chevon is the meat of a goat.
items.hint3: Meat can only be taken after slaughter. Which of the three products can a farmer collect again and again from the same live animal?
items.solution:
Answer: B. I and III

Some animal products come from the living animal and can be collected many times, while others need the animal to be slaughtered. Eggs are laid by living hens, and milk comes from living cows or goats. Chevon is goat meat, which is obtained only after the goat is killed.

How to tell:
I. Egg: from a living hen, so included.
II. Chevon: goat meat, from a slaughtered goat, so left out.
III. Milk: from a living animal, so included.

Why not the others:
A. I and II: includes chevon, which needs slaughter.
C. II and III: includes chevon and leaves out eggs.
D. I, II and III: includes chevon, which needs slaughter.

Exam tip: learn the meat names: beef (cattle), chevon (goat), mutton (sheep), pork (pig), veal (calf). All meat and hides need slaughter, while eggs, milk, wool and honey come from living animals.

items.hint1: Water is taken back from leftover feed after digestion is mostly over. Think about where that happens along the gut.
items.hint2: The duodenum is at the start of the small intestine, where food is digested. The rectum at the end mainly stores faeces before they leave the body.
items.hint3: Two parts of the large intestine remain. In the syllabus, one is a blind sac for fermenting fibre and the other is where faeces are formed. Which one removes the water?
items.solution:
Answer: D. colon

After digestion and absorption of nutrients, the undigested residue passes into the large intestine. In the colon, water is absorbed from it, so the residue becomes firmer and is formed into faeces.

How to tell: in the syllabus, water absorption from undigested feed is the job of the colon, the main part of the large intestine.

Why not the others:
A. caecum: in the syllabus its role is fermenting fibre with microbes, not the main absorption of water, even though some water is taken up there.
B. rectum: it stores faeces before they are passed out.
C. duodenum: it digests food with enzymes and bile, and absorbs nutrients rather than water from waste.

Exam tip: learn the gut parts in order with one job each: duodenum digests, ileum absorbs nutrients, caecum ferments fibre, colon absorbs water, rectum stores faeces.

items.hint1: This is an 'except' question. Decide for each statement whether the rumen really does it.
items.hint2: The rumen is the large first stomach where feed is held and microbes break down fibre. Its microbes make some vitamins, but ask which ones.
items.hint3: Rumen microbes make B vitamins and vitamin K. Check statement III against that, then choose the option that lists only the false statements.
items.solution:
Answer: C. III only

The rumen is the largest compartment of a ruminant's stomach. It holds swallowed feed for a while, and its microbes ferment the fibre. The microbes also make B vitamins and vitamin K. Vitamins A and D are not made there: vitamin A comes from green feed and vitamin D is made in the skin in sunlight.

How to tell:
I. temporary storage of feed: true, so not an exception.
II. fermentation of feed: true, so not an exception.
III. synthesis of vitamin A and D: false, so this is the exception.

Why not the others:
A. I only: storage of feed is a real rumen function.
B. II only: fermentation is the rumen's main function.
D. I and III: statement I is a real function, so it is not an exception.

Exam tip: for 'except' questions with Roman numerals, mark each statement true or false first, then pick the option that lists exactly the false ones. For the rumen, remember: storage, fermentation, B vitamins and vitamin K.

items.hint1: This is a 'not' question. Think about the two stages of artificial insemination: taking semen from the male, then placing it in the female.
items.hint2: Three of the options are the standard ways of collecting semen from a male. One tool belongs to the other stage.
items.hint3: Which of these instruments is a thin tube used to put semen into the female's reproductive tract, rather than to collect it?
items.solution:
Answer: C. use of catheter

Artificial insemination has two main stages: collecting semen from the male, then depositing it in the female. The syllabus lists three ways of collecting semen: the artificial vagina, massage, and electro-ejaculation. A catheter is a thin tube used in the second stage, to place semen in the female.

How to tell: ask whether each method takes semen out of the male. Only the catheter does not.

Why not the others:
A. use of artificial vagina: a standard collection method, in which the male mounts and ejaculates into it.
B. massage: a collection method in which the reproductive glands are massaged to release semen.
D. electro ejaculation: a collection method using a mild electrical stimulus.

Exam tip: in artificial insemination questions, sort each tool by stage: collection (artificial vagina, massage, electro-ejaculation), storage (liquid nitrogen), insemination (catheter or inseminating gun).

items.hint1: Heat stress happens when an animal is too hot. Think about how an animal changes its eating and drinking to cope with heat.
items.hint2: A hot animal drinks more water to cool down and eats less feed, because digesting feed produces body heat.
items.hint3: Heat stress harms breeding as well as feeding. For each of the two options left, ask whether heat stress would push that result up or down.
items.solution:
Answer: D. reduced milk production

When an animal is too hot, it eats less feed and uses energy to cool itself. With less feed and energy available, production falls, so dairy animals give less milk.

How to tell: heat stress lowers feed intake, and lower feed intake means lower output of milk, eggs and growth.

Why not the others:
A. increased feed intake: heat stress lowers appetite, so feed intake falls.
B. reduced water intake: hot animals drink more water, not less.
C. increased little size: heat stress lowers fertility, so litter size tends to fall, not rise.

Exam tip: for heat stress questions, remember the pattern: water intake goes up, while feed intake, growth, milk, eggs and fertility go down.

items.hint1: The question gives the space each bird needs and the size of the house. Start by finding the total floor area.
items.hint2: Floor area of a rectangle is length × breadth. Then share that area among the birds, each needing 0.36 m².
items.hint3: Divide the floor area by the space for one bird. One option is just the floor area itself, which is not a number of birds.
items.solution:
Answer: D. 500

The number of birds a house can hold is its floor area divided by the floor space each bird needs. The word 'children' in the question is a misprint for chickens.

How to tell:
Floor area = 9 m × 20 m
Floor area = 180 m²
Number of birds = 180 m² ÷ 0.36 m² per bird
Number of birds = 500 birds

Why not the others:
A. 65: does not come from dividing 180 m² by 0.36 m².
B. 81: does not come from the correct working either.
C. 180: this is the floor area in m², not the number of birds.

Exam tip: for stocking sums, find the total area first, then divide by the space per animal. Check that your answer is a number of animals, not the area you started with.

items.hint1: Think about the climate in West Africa and what hot, crowded birds need most inside their house.
items.hint2: Open sides let in air and wind, so they cannot be for shielding birds from wind or for keeping them warm.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one is about air moving through the house and the other is about removing dirt. Which do open sides provide?
items.solution:
Answer: C. promotes adequate ventilation

In a hot climate, poultry houses need good ventilation, which means fresh air moving through the house. Open sides, usually covered with wire mesh, let air flow freely, carrying away heat, moisture and ammonia from the droppings.

How to tell: open sides let air pass through, so their benefit is ventilation.

Why not the others:
A. protect birds from strong winds: open sides let wind in, so they do not shield birds from it.
B. keep the bird warm: open sides cool the house rather than warm it.
D. facilitates easy cleaning: cleaning depends on the floor and litter, not on open sides.

Exam tip: for questions on house design, match each feature to its purpose: open sides for ventilation, wide roof overhang to keep out rain and sun, concrete floor for easy cleaning, wire mesh to keep out predators.

items.hint1: Each option is the name for the male of a farm animal. First work out which animal each word belongs to.
items.hint2: In Agricultural Science, wool is the soft, curly coat sheared from sheep. Birds give feathers, and pigs have coarse bristles.
items.hint3: Once you drop the bird and the pig, you are left with a male goat or rabbit and a male sheep. Which of those two is the wool animal?
items.solution:
Answer: C. ram

In the syllabus, wool is the product of sheep. It is the thick coat that is sheared off the living animal each year, and a ram is simply a male sheep, so it carries the same wool as a ewe.

How to tell: match each male name to its animal. Boar is a male pig, buck is a male goat or rabbit, ram is a male sheep and cock is a male fowl. Only the sheep is the wool animal.

Why not the others:
A. boar: a male pig, whose coat is coarse bristles, not wool.
B. buck: a male goat or rabbit, whose coat is hair or fur rather than the wool the syllabus links to sheep.
D. cock: a male fowl, which is covered in feathers, not wool.

Exam tip: learn the male, female and young names of each farm animal together (sheep: ram, ewe, lamb; goat: buck, doe, kid; pig: boar, sow, piglet; fowl: cock, hen, chick). Many product questions are really asking you to decode these names.

items.hint1: Before choosing, decide what kind of organism causes each disease: a virus, a fungus, a protozoan or a bacterium.
items.hint2: Drugs like sulpha drugs and sulphur ointments act on living organisms such as protozoa and fungi. Viral diseases of poultry are not cured by drugs, they are prevented by vaccination.
items.hint3: One of the three diseases is caused by a virus. Remove every option that includes it and see what remains.
items.solution:
Answer: A. I and II

Sulphur-containing drugs work against living disease organisms such as protozoa and fungi. Viruses are not killed by these drugs, so in the syllabus viral poultry diseases are controlled by vaccination and hygiene, not treated with drugs.

How to tell: coccidiosis is caused by a protozoan (Eimeria) and is treated with sulpha drugs such as sulphaquinoxaline. Ringworm (favus in fowls) is caused by a fungus and can be treated with sulphur-based ointments. Fowl pox is caused by a virus, so it has no drug cure and is prevented by vaccination. That leaves I and II.

Why not the others:
B. I and III: includes fowl pox, a viral disease that sulphur drugs do not cure.
C. II and III: includes fowl pox and leaves out coccidiosis, the disease sulpha drugs are best known for treating.
D. I, II and III: includes fowl pox, which is controlled by vaccination, not drugs.

Exam tip: for any treatment question, first sort each disease by its cause. Protozoan and bacterial diseases are treated with drugs, fungal ones with antifungal or sulphur preparations, and viral ones (fowl pox, Newcastle disease) are prevented by vaccination.

items.hint1: The question asks for the most important benefit, not just a true one. Think about how bees help the whole food supply, not only the beekeeper.
items.hint2: Beeswax is a real product, but it is a small by-product of the hive. Research use and 'raw materials' are vague or minor compared with what bees do outside the hive every day.
items.hint3: Compare the value of a hive product with the value of what bees do for the flowers of many crops as they feed. Which helps far more people?
items.solution:
Answer: C. act as agent of pollination

As bees move from flower to flower collecting nectar, they carry pollen with them. This pollination lets many crops, such as fruits, vegetables and oil crops, set fruit and seed, so it supports far more food than any single hive product can.

How to tell: a hive gives honey and a little wax to one beekeeper, but pollination raises the yield of crops on farms all around the hive. That is why textbooks rank pollination as the most important service bees give to humans.

Why not the others:
A. produce beeswax: a useful product, but only a minor by-product of beekeeping.
B. provide raw materials: too vague, and any raw materials from the hive are worth far less than pollination.
D. be used for research purposes: a small, specialised use, not a major benefit to most people.

Exam tip: when a question asks for the 'most important' or 'main' role of something, choose the benefit that reaches the widest number of people or crops, not a side product.

items.hint1: Separate food crops, which are mostly eaten at home, from cash crops, which are grown mainly to sell, often to other countries.
items.hint2: Maize and yam are staple foods eaten daily in most West African homes, with little left over to sell abroad.
items.hint3: Between the two crops left, think about which one is dried, packed and shipped abroad in large quantities, and which one is usually eaten fresh by the family soon after harvest.
items.solution:
Answer: B. cocoa

An export crop is grown mainly to be sold to other countries, earning foreign exchange. West Africa, especially Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Nigeria, produces a large share of the world's cocoa, and most of it is shipped abroad.

How to tell: cocoa beans are hardly eaten locally as food. They are dried and exported to be made into chocolate and cocoa drinks. The other three crops are mainly food for people at home.

Why not the others:
A. maize: a staple food and feed crop, mostly used within West Africa.
C. yam: a staple food crop, grown mainly for local eating.
D. plantain: a staple food crop, mostly sold and eaten locally.

Exam tip: in West Africa, the export crops the syllabus lists are the cash crops: cocoa, rubber, cotton, oil palm produce, groundnut, coffee and cashew. Staples like maize, yam, cassava and plantain are food crops.

items.hint1: Cost of production per unit is total production cost divided by the number of units produced. Find those two figures in the passage.
items.hint2: Production cost is what it took to produce the eggs. Money spent after production, such as selling costs, and money received from sales are not part of it.
items.hint3: Use the total cost stated for producing the trays and the number of trays produced. Divide one by the other.
items.solution:
Answer: B. ₦700.00

Cost of production per unit is the total cost of producing the goods shared equally over every unit produced. It does not matter what later happens to each tray, whether it is sold or eaten, because each one cost the same to produce.

How to tell:
Total cost of production = ₦350,000.00
Trays produced = 500
Cost per tray = ₦350,000.00 ÷ 500
Cost per tray = ₦700.00

Why not the others:
A. ₦640.00: this subtracts the ₦30,000.00 marketing cost from the production cost, (₦350,000 − ₦30,000) ÷ 500, which has no meaning.
C. ₦760.00: this adds the marketing cost, (₦350,000 + ₦30,000) ÷ 500, but marketing is a selling cost, not a production cost.
D. ₦1,000.00: this divides the sales income, ₦500,000 ÷ 500, which is revenue, not cost.

Exam tip: in farm account questions, sort each money figure first into production cost, marketing cost or revenue. Cost of production per unit uses only the production cost and the total number produced.

items.hint1: Read what happened to the eggs before sales. Not every tray produced reached the market.
items.hint2: The family's share is given as a percentage of total output. Turn that percentage into a number of trays first.
items.hint3: Work out 1% of the total output, then take it away from the total. Check your answer is smaller than the number produced, but only slightly.
items.solution:
Answer: C. 495

The trays sold are what is left of the total output after the family has taken its share. The family's share is a percentage of the whole output, so it must be changed into a number of trays before subtracting.

How to tell:
Total output = 500 trays
Family consumption = 1% of 500 = 1/100 × 500 = 5 trays
Trays sold = 500 − 5
Trays sold = 495 trays

Why not the others:
A. 4000: more than the 500 trays produced, so it cannot be the number sold.
B. 490: this removes 10 trays, which is 2% of 500, not 1%.
D. 500: this is the total produced and ignores the trays the family ate before sales.

Exam tip: when a passage says part of the output was consumed, lost or given away before sales, subtract that part from total output to get the quantity sold. Convert any percentage into units first.

items.hint1: Price depends on two things: how much buyers want the produce and how much they value its quality. Ask how each function affects one of these.
items.hint2: Grading sorts produce by quality so that better produce can be sold at a higher price, and processing adds value by turning raw produce into a more useful product.
items.hint3: You already know two of the functions help. Now decide whether making more buyers aware of the produce, and so raising demand, can also help the farmer ask a better price.
items.solution:
Answer: D. I, II and III

A farmer gets a better price when buyers want the produce more or value it more. Each of the three functions does one of these, so each can help the farmer fix a better price.

How to tell: advertisement makes more buyers aware of the produce, which raises demand, and higher demand supports a higher price. Processing turns raw produce into a more valuable product, such as cassava into garri, so it sells for more. Grading sorts produce into quality classes so the best grade can be sold at a higher price.

Why not the others:
A. I and II: leaves out grading, which lets top-quality produce earn a higher price.
B. I and III: leaves out processing, which adds value to the produce.
C. II and III: leaves out advertisement, which raises demand and so supports a better price.

Exam tip: for 'which functions help' questions, test each statement on its own against the goal in the stem. If every statement passes, the answer is the option that includes all of them.
